task.goal: Help residents compare two municipal waste-sorting instructions that use different terms.
hard_constraints: One page of printed guidance and one volunteer translator; no claim of legal authority.
Do not merge conflicting rules silently; preserve source dates and exceptions.
Test whether readers sort unfamiliar items correctly and know when to ask.
task.available_resources: Two official leaflets and a list of common questions.
task.expected_result: A clear comparison aid and update rule.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Parallel terminology crosswalk
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Create a one-page table that lets residents compare the two vocabularies without treating them as interchangeable. Each row pairs a term from leaflet A with its closest counterpart in leaflet B, gives a plain-language meaning, and records whether their coverage matches, overlaps, or conflicts. Where there is no counterpart, say so. Keep exceptions alongside the relevant term rather than in distant footnotes. The mechanism is explicit comparison: readers can see when different words describe the same instruction and when similar words conceal different rules.

The volunteer translator checks both original terms and plain-language explanations, using the common-question list to prioritize confusing distinctions. Include each leaflet’s title, issuing body, date, and applicable area if stated; label missing dates as unknown. Mark the aid as an unofficial comparison. Conflicting or unclear entries say “check before sorting,” with any clarification route actually supplied by the leaflets.

This requires enough space to retain consequential exceptions in readable type. It assumes most confusion concerns terminology; translation alone cannot resolve policy differences. Update rule: when either leaflet changes, recheck every paired entry and exception, replace the printed page, and record the new source dates. Do not describe either source as superseded without evidence.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the draft with the two leaflets alone using a few residents and six unfamiliar items whose treatment is supported by the sources. Include an exception and an unresolved conflict. Ask for the destination, the supporting instruction, and whether clarification is needed. Prewrite answers from the leaflets; score unresolved cases as requiring a question, not a guessed bin. Reject or revise the crosswalk if it increases confident errors, hides a conflict, or fails to improve interpretation of differently named categories. This small check can expose problems but cannot establish population-wide effectiveness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A source-separated decision path
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Build a one-page decision tree that starts with the situation governing the instruction, then guides residents through the distinctions actually stated in the leaflets. If the sources specify different areas, services, or collection arrangements, make that the first branch. If applicability cannot be established, route the reader to “ask which instruction applies.” Within each source’s branch, ask short questions about relevant item characteristics, preparation, or exceptions. Retain that leaflet’s category names at the endpoints.

The mechanism is procedural: readers answer observable questions instead of first translating category labels. The volunteer translator converts source wording into short questions and checks that every endpoint and exception remains traceable to the corresponding leaflet. Use the common questions to choose the most useful paths. Print the source titles and dates, explain that the page is unofficial, and visibly flag conflicting instructions rather than selecting a winner.

This works only if the rules can be expressed as a small number of reliable questions. If the tree becomes cramped or depends on facts residents cannot observe, it is unsuitable. Update rule: a changed leaflet triggers a review of the applicability branch and every affected question, endpoint, and exception; replace the page with its revised source dates.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the tree with a simple two-column summary of the same instructions. Ask a few residents to sort unfamiliar items covering ordinary paths, an exception, and uncertain applicability. Record their answers and the branches they followed. Check both correct sorting under the applicable source and stopping to ask when the source cannot be selected. The mechanism is undermined if readers repeatedly choose the wrong first branch, cannot answer a question, or reach a confident endpoint for an unresolved case. Inspect the paths before attributing mistakes to translation.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Contrast pairs that teach rule boundaries
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use one printed page to teach residents how small item differences change the instruction. Select a few common questions and turn them into paired examples: two items or conditions differing in one feature that the leaflets explicitly treat differently. Beside each pair, state the deciding feature and show leaflet A’s and leaflet B’s instructions separately. Use text examples drawn from the supplied materials; do not invent disposal rules. Finish with a short transfer prompt: “Which feature matters here? Does your leaflet cover it? If not, ask.”

The mechanism is learning through contrast. Residents practice identifying the rule boundary, which may help them classify unfamiliar items beyond the examples shown. The volunteer translator checks the examples and explains unfamiliar terms while preserving original category labels. Include source titles, dates, relevant exceptions, an unofficial-status statement, and a visible indication wherever the sources disagree. Use only clarification contacts already provided in the materials.

This requires the leaflets to contain a few clear, generalizable distinctions. Its main limit is overgeneralization: examples may suggest broader rules than the sources support. Update rule: when either source changes, revalidate every example and its stated boundary, replace affected pairs, and print the revised dates. If too few valid contrasts exist, use a direct comparison table instead.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Give a few residents either the contrast page with a brief volunteer explanation or an equally brief explanation using a conventional category list. Then present unfamiliar items that share the relevant features but were absent from the examples, including one exception and one case the sources do not resolve. Ask residents to explain the deciding feature and identify when to ask. Revise or reject the approach if it improves recall of examples but fails on unfamiliar items, encourages unsupported analogies, or reduces appropriate requests for clarification. Keep this an exploratory user check, not a claimed effectiveness result.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A teach-back sheet that exposes misunderstandings
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make the volunteer’s correction of residents’ interpretations the main mechanism. Use one printed page containing two clearly separated source panels and a short teach-back exercise. Each panel retains its leaflet’s category terms, explains the distinctions prioritized by the common-question list, and places consequential exceptions beside the relevant instruction. Include source titles, dates or “date unknown,” and stated applicability. Label the page “Unofficial comparison”; display disagreements explicitly without choosing a winner.

During a brief conversation, the volunteer asks the resident to explain what each leaflet would require for an item and why. The volunteer checks that explanation against the originals, identifies any lost condition or mistaken equivalence, and asks the resident to explain the corrected distinction using another example. Finish by having the resident explain when they would ask for help: uncertain applicability, conflicting instructions, or an item the sources do not cover. Use only clarification routes actually provided in the materials; otherwise acknowledge that no route is supplied.

What changes the outcome is feedback on the resident’s interpretation before it becomes a sorting habit. This could reveal misunderstandings that a readable translation alone leaves hidden. It requires the volunteer to understand both texts and residents to have time for a short exchange. It cannot settle policy ambiguity, and benefit may depend on continued volunteer availability. Keep the originals available for checking; if essential exceptions cannot fit legibly, narrow the page’s stated coverage.

Update rule: whenever either leaflet changes, recheck both panels and the exercise prompts, replace the page, and show the revised source dates. Do not infer that the newer leaflet overrides the other.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Give a few residents the same sheet, with either a brief read-through or an equally timed teach-back conversation. Then independently ask them to sort unfamiliar, source-supported items and identify when to ask, including an exception and an unresolved case. Establish expected answers from the originals beforehand. Revise or reject the mechanism if feedback fails to reduce interpretation errors, creates confident guesses about unresolved cases, or requires explanations the volunteer cannot reliably provide. This checks feasibility and exposes failures; it does not establish general effectiveness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Preempt misleading shortcuts
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Create a one-page comparison aid organized around tempting but unsupported shortcuts, such as assuming that similar category names cover the same items or that a newer date automatically makes the other leaflet irrelevant. The mechanism is preventive error correction: explain why a shortcut can fail before residents use it, and replace it with a specific checking habit. Unlike teaching category definitions, this targets how residents decide whether an apparent match is trustworthy.

The volunteer translator uses the common questions to identify up to three plausible shortcuts, retaining only those for which the supplied leaflets demonstrate a consequential problem. Each entry contains the tempting assumption, brief supporting excerpts from both leaflets, a plain-language explanation of the difference, and the condition or exception residents must check. Present the two sources separately throughout. Close with explicit reasons to ask: uncertain applicability, conflicting instructions, or missing coverage. Include any clarification route supplied by the materials; acknowledge if none is supplied.

Print source titles, dates or “date unknown,” stated applicability, and “Unofficial comparison; no legal authority.” Preserve relevant exceptions beside each entry. If space is insufficient, narrow and label the page’s coverage. This requires only the leaflets, question list, one page, and the translator. It assumes misleading shortcuts contribute to confusion; the question list may not establish that. If the sources provide no defensible examples, this approach is unsuitable.

Update rule: when either leaflet changes, recheck every quoted passage, correction, and exception, replace the page, and display the revised source dates. Never infer precedence from date alone.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the page with an equally brief, source-separated summary. Ask a few residents to sort unfamiliar items supported by the leaflets, including an exception, and assess an unresolved case. Establish expected answers from the originals beforehand. Record correct destinations, confident errors, and appropriate requests for clarification. Reject or revise the approach if residents repeat the warned-against shortcuts, become indiscriminately hesitant on clear cases, or perform no better than the summary. This is a small feasibility check, not evidence of general effectiveness.

EXPAND.title: Item-first answer index
EXPAND.proposal:
Remove the requirement to understand both category systems before finding an answer. Use the common-question list to select a small set of item names residents already use. Print an alphabetical, one-page index with each item followed by leaflet A’s instruction and leaflet B’s instruction, retaining each original category label, preparation requirement, and relevant exception. Explicitly mark disagreements and omissions; an omission does not establish permission or prohibition. This mechanism reduces the translation residents must perform before acting.

The volunteer translator prepares the index directly from the two leaflets. Print their titles, dates, and stated applicability, marking missing information as unknown, and label the page “Unofficial comparison.” Residents find their item, check its condition and which source applies, then follow that source’s instruction. If the item is absent, its condition differs, applicability is uncertain, or applicable sources conflict, the page directs them to ask rather than infer an answer from a similar item. Use a clarification route only if the supplied materials provide one; otherwise state that the materials do not identify one.

This assumes common questions cover enough actual decisions to make a short index useful. It sacrifices broad coverage to provide precise answers with little vocabulary learning. Keep entries readable rather than expanding to fit every question. When either leaflet changes, the volunteer rechecks every indexed instruction and exception, replaces the page, and records the revised source dates. An unresolved entry remains visibly unresolved.
EXPAND.experiment: The volunteer runs a first trial with four to six residents, comparing the index with the prior terminology crosswalk on matched unfamiliar items. Include indexed items, a condition-sensitive exception, an unlisted item, and a conflict. Prepare source-supported answers beforehand. Record correct sorting, appropriate requests for help, lookup time, and unsupported answers for unlisted items. Stop and revise if an exception is lost or the index encourages confident extrapolation. Reject the approach if its faster lookup does not improve correct decisions after accounting for reduced coverage and additional requests for help. This small trial can reveal failures, not establish general effectiveness.

EXPAND.title: Evidence-backed teach-back with the volunteer
EXPAND.proposal:
Use the volunteer to detect and correct residents’ interpretations before those interpretations guide sorting. Prepare one printed page containing short, source-separated instruction excerpts selected through the common questions, with space beside each for “What I would do” and “When I would ask.” Keep original category labels, source dates, applicability, and consequential exceptions beside the excerpts. Mark conflicts explicitly and identify the page as an unofficial learning aid.

The volunteer asks a resident to explain an instruction in their own words and point to the words supporting their action. The volunteer checks that explanation against the original leaflet, corrects any unsupported interpretation, and asks the resident to explain it again. The mechanism is a feedback loop that exposes individual misunderstandings; it does not depend on residents noticing their own confusion. The resident keeps the page as a reminder and uses its source references when comparing later instructions.

Teaching includes a specific action-versus-handoff rule: act when the applicable source explicitly supports the item and condition; ask when applicability, an exception, or a disagreement remains unresolved. The volunteer translates and checks comprehension but does not decide policy. Questions beyond the leaflets remain unanswered and use any clarification route supplied there.

This requires residents to have brief access to the single volunteer and assumes spoken explanation is practical. It may create queues and cannot guarantee later retention. Following a source change, the volunteer checks every excerpt and teaching prompt, replaces the page with revised dates, and repeats affected explanations when residents return.
EXPAND.experiment: The volunteer pilots this with four to six residents against an equally timed explanation of the prior contrast-pair page. Test without further coaching, using a source-supported close pair on opposite sides of the act-versus-ask boundary and one unfamiliar transfer item. Check sorting, the act-or-ask choice, and the cited reason. Record volunteer minutes and residents’ ability to use the page independently. Stop if correction introduces an unsupported rule. Retain the approach only if it improves decisions enough to justify the additional interaction; accurate repetition followed by poor transfer would falsify its proposed benefit.

EXPAND.title: A comparison-and-question slip for unresolved cases
EXPAND.proposal:
Make unresolved differences actionable by helping residents formulate a precise question. Use one printed page with a compact comparison section drawn from the common questions and a reusable question template: item and condition; relevant wording from leaflet A; relevant wording from leaflet B; each source’s date and applicability; and the exact uncertainty needing clarification. Preserve original terms, exceptions, and disagreements. Label the page as an unofficial comparison with no legal authority.

The mechanism is better handoff: residents need not reconcile the complete terminology systems to identify what information is missing. For clearly covered items, they read both source entries and follow the instruction whose applicability is established. For a gap or conflict, they mark the relevant entries and complete the question template with help from the volunteer translator. For example, the question can ask which instruction applies to the stated collection arrangement, rather than asking what an unfamiliar category word means.

The volunteer checks the completed question against both leaflets and removes any assumed answer. Residents use a clarification route only when one is supplied in the materials. If none is supplied, the page explicitly records that the handoff cannot yet be completed; the volunteer cannot substitute an authoritative ruling. No disposal destination is invented while an answer is pending.

This approach assumes some confusion persists even after clear comparison. Its benefit depends on access to clarification and may be limited to producing a usable question. When either leaflet changes, the volunteer rechecks the comparison and outstanding question wording, replaces the page, and records revised source dates. An undocumented response does not silently become a printed rule.
EXPAND.experiment: The volunteer compares this page with the prior crosswalk’s ordinary “check before sorting” instruction in a four-to-six-resident trial. Include a clearly resolved unfamiliar item, a closely related unresolved case, and another unfamiliar case. Score correct sorting and appropriate handoff, then inspect whether each question contains enough source information to identify the unresolved issue. Record completion time and unnecessary handoffs. Stop if the template steers residents toward an unsupported answer. Reject it if question quality does not improve enough to justify the added effort, or if it causes residents to defer straightforward decisions. Without an available clarification route, report only question readiness, not successful resolution.

EXPAND.title: Crosswalk with explicit limits on each match
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the parallel terminology crosswalk, preserving its paired original terms, plain-language meanings, match/overlap/conflict labels, source titles and dates, applicability, adjacent exceptions, and unofficial status. Change the working procedure: the volunteer must qualify each pairing with the item conditions for which the comparison is supported. A broad category match cannot serve as a sorting instruction outside those conditions. This addresses the risk that residents interpret a vocabulary correspondence as permission to transfer every rule between sources.

Use the common questions to choose a readable set of rows on one printed page. For each, the volunteer checks both leaflets and states the supported boundary, including preparation requirements and consequential exceptions. Residents use a row only when their item and condition fall within that boundary and the applicable source is established. Otherwise, they ask; disagreements remain visible. Use only clarification routes supplied in the materials, and state when none is identified. The volunteer translates but cannot settle policy.

If a row cannot retain its necessary qualifications in readable space, omit the pairing and list that topic as requiring consultation of the original leaflets or clarification. This sacrifices coverage to reduce unsupported transfer. It assumes the leaflets contain sufficiently explicit boundaries; uncertain wording remains uncertain. When either leaflet changes, the volunteer rechecks all pairings and exceptions, records the source dates, and replaces the page. Until rechecked, affected pairings are marked unavailable rather than retained as current guidance.
EXPAND.experiment: The volunteer prepares a bounded trial with four to six residents, comparing this page with the original crosswalk on matched unfamiliar items. Include a close pair consisting of a clearly covered condition and a nearby condition requiring clarification, plus another unfamiliar item and a source conflict. Prepare source-supported scoring before the trial; unresolved cases require asking, not a guessed destination. Record correct sorting, appropriate requests for help, confident unsupported transfers, lookup time, and unnecessary referrals. Inspect every printed qualification against both leaflets. Stop and revise if a missing exception or overbroad match permits an unsupported action. Keep the added boundaries only if they reduce unsupported transfers without making clearly covered decisions substantially harder. This trial can identify failures, not establish general effectiveness.

EXPAND.title: Decision path with a recoverable “cannot tell” branch
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the source-separated decision path. Keep applicability first, source-specific category names, short questions derived from the leaflets, visible conflicts, exceptions, source dates, and an unofficial-status statement. Add a working rule at every consequential question: “Cannot tell from the item or these instructions” must lead to a specific unresolved question, never to a default yes or no. This closes a gap between detecting an unusable question during testing and helping a resident who encounters it during ordinary use.

The volunteer builds the one-page path from the two leaflets, prioritizing the common questions. For each uncertain branch, print a short identifier and the missing fact—for example, which collection arrangement applies, without inventing arrangements absent from the sources. Residents can retain the page and identify the branch where they stopped. They resume only when the missing fact is established from the materials or through a clarification route supplied there; they then follow the remaining questions rather than jumping to a remembered endpoint.

The resident retains responsibility for the unresolved decision until a named contact actually accepts the question; merely attempting contact does not resolve it. If contact is unavailable or interrupted, the branch remains unresolved. The volunteer can explain wording and help formulate the question but cannot authorize disposal or invent temporary handling instructions.

This needs observable distinctions and enough page space for readable questions and exceptions. If uncertainty branches make the path too dense, the volunteer reduces its stated coverage and directs omitted cases to the original leaflets or clarification. Compared with the original tree, this adds stopping points and potentially more requests for help, but avoids forced guesses and repeated explanation after interruption. A changed leaflet triggers review of applicability, affected questions, endpoints, and exceptions; affected paths remain unavailable until checked, and the replacement records both source dates.
EXPAND.experiment: The volunteer tests the revised and original paths with four to six residents using matched unfamiliar cases. Include a close pair where an observable fact supports sorting in one case but the necessary fact is unavailable in the other, plus another unfamiliar item and an exception. Score source-supported sorting, appropriate stopping and asking, unnecessary referrals, and time. For one unresolved case, interrupt the explanation briefly, then check whether the resident can identify the missing fact and resume from the correct branch when supplied with source-supported information. Stop and revise if any unknown answer reaches a disposal endpoint or any resumed path bypasses an exception. Retain the change only if it reduces guessing or restart errors enough to justify additional reading and referrals. Successful clarification cannot be claimed if no usable contact exists.
